finding: `let window = &rest[..rest.len().min(400)]` slices a &str by BYTE index. If byte 400 of the window lands inside a multi-byte UTF-8 char the test PANICS with 'byte index 400 is not a char boundary' instead of reporting a drift. validate.rs currently holds 161 non-ASCII bytes and ref_check.rs 79 (em dashes / ellipses in doc comments and messages); I verified none currently sits in the 380..420 window of any `ValidationError::` occurrence, so it passes today, but any future message or doc-comment edit that shifts one there converts the humanisation guard into an unrelated panic. Use floor_char_boundary / char_indices().take_while instead.

VALIDATE_SRC is `include_str!("validate.rs")`, i.e. the scanner also scans this file's own `mod tests` and the humanisation_contract module. A future test fixture that constructs `ValidationError::at("semantic", "WORKFLOW_X", ...)` inside a #[cfg(test)] block would be counted as a production emit site, forcing a bogus VALIDATION_CODES + validationCopy.ts entry for a code the server can never emit. I confirmed the two existing self-references (the doc comment at 1926 and the assert string at 2014) do NOT produce false positives, because their first literal is not one of schema/semantic/security. Failure mode is noisy (test fails), not silent.

no findings for this angle beyond the byte-slice panic logged under correctness-logic: the cross-file `include_str!` of validationCopy.ts fails at COMPILE time if the file is moved or renamed (loud), and if the file is emptied or truncated the `unhumanised` assertion lists all 41 codes and fails loudly. There is no swallowed I/O and no `unwrap` on a runtime value in the added code.

The humanisation half of the guard is a raw substring search over the WHOLE file: `!UI_COPY_SRC.contains(&format!("\"{code}\""))`. It does not check that the code is a key of `HUMAN_COPY`. Concrete failure: delete `"WORKFLOW_TOOL_NO_TOOL": () => ...` from HUMAN_COPY but leave the code quoted anywhere else in the file (a comment, a deprecated list, a doc block) and this test stays green; `humaniseFinding` then hits its `if (!copy) return finding.message` fallback (validationCopy.ts:172-174) and the raw wire message reaches the author — exactly the property the test claims to guarantee. The TS-side test cannot catch it either, because it iterates `HUMANISED_CODES = Object.keys(HUMAN_COPY)`, which no longer contains the code. A structural check (parse the keys, or have the TS test assert against a generated list) would close it.

no vacuity finding: I specifically checked for the 'cross-file test that silently scans zero items' failure. The test has an explicit `assert!(!emitted.is_empty(), ...)` self-check AND, more importantly, the bidirectional `stale` assertion (registered - emitted must be empty) means a scanner that degrades to finding a SUBSET of emit sites also fails loudly with the missing codes named. Verified empirically that it currently finds all 41. Rejecting my initial suspicion that this is a vacuous guard.

The scanner's source set is a hardcoded two-file list (VALIDATE_SRC + REF_CHECK_SRC at 1916-1917) while the emitters `ValidationError::{err,at,warn}` are `pub(crate)` (441/450/466) and the struct's fields are `pub`. Any OTHER module in the crate that starts emitting workflow findings (a future policy_check.rs, or a direct `ValidationError { code: .., .. }` struct literal) is invisible to `emitted_codes`: its code is neither registry-checked nor humanisation-checked, so it silently reaches the builder as a raw wire message. There is no compile-time seam forcing a new emitting file into the scan — the next contributor has to know to edit line 1917.

Two closed filters silently DROP emit sites rather than failing: the layer allowlist `matches!(literals[0].as_str(), "schema"|"semantic"|"security")` (1965) and the SCREAMING_SNAKE charset filter on the code (1966). Failure mode: introduce a fourth layer (say "policy"), emit `WORKFLOW_NEW_THING` from it and forget the registry — `emitted` never sees the code, `unregistered` is empty, `unhumanised` is empty, the test passes, and the builder shows the raw validator message. The `stale` direction only rescues the case where the author DID register the code, which is not the case the guard exists for. The comment at 1961-1963 states the drop-rather-than-false-positive tradeoff but not that it re-opens the silent hole.

Adding one validation code now requires edits in three places: the emit site, `VALIDATION_CODES` (355), and `HUMAN_COPY` in validationCopy.ts. The registry is a middleman that adds no guarantee the test could not get directly — `emitted` is already derived from source, so comparing `emitted` against the UI copy would enforce the same INV-1 property with one fewer hand-maintained closed list. Its only extra value is the duplicate/shape check in `validation_codes_registry_is_well_formed` and the grouping comments.

The `400` window is a magic constant justified only as 'a generous bound'. Nothing detects the case where a call's first two string literals fall OUTSIDE it (e.g. a long `//` comment inserted between `ValidationError::at(` and the layer argument): the site is then silently skipped, and the miss only surfaces if the code was already registered (via `stale`). Either derive the bound (scan to the matching close paren) or assert that a window ending mid-call is an error.

no further findings for this angle: the per-group comments in VALIDATION_CODES (`// validate.rs — prompts`, `// ref_check.rs — type-aware reference checking`) are hand-maintained and unchecked, so a code that moves between files leaves a stale comment. I verified every grouping is currently ACCURATE (all 8 ref_check codes really are emitted from ref_check.rs, the other 33 from validate.rs), and a stale comment has no behavioural consequence — rejecting as style.

`pub const VALIDATION_CODES` has no production consumer: `grep -rn VALIDATION_CODES src-app/ --include=*.rs --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx` matches only validate.rs itself (the const, its `use super::` in the test module, and the two test bodies). It is a `pub` API-surface item read exclusively by #[cfg(test)] code, and because it is `pub` the dead_code lint will never flag it. CODING_GUIDELINES §15 requires a new public item to have a production caller; either make it `pub(crate)`/private with `#[cfg(test)]`-adjacent scope, or wire it into a real consumer (e.g. have `workflow_mcp::validate_workflow` document the code set from it).

`let mut chars = window[open..].char_indices().peekable();` — `peek()` is never called anywhere in the loop (the only consumption is `chars.next()` at 1940 and 1955). The `.peekable()` adapter is dead and misleads a reader into looking for lookahead logic that does not exist.
